# Inventory Management for D2C Brands: Stock, Bundles & Returns


Having an inventory management capability for a direct-to-consumer (D2C) brand means more than just knowing how many products you have in your warehouse. Whether orders funnel through your website, marketplaces, social commerce platforms and other sales channels you will soon find maintaining stock accuracy more difficult with order handling.


Toss in product bundles, exchanges, returns, defective items and marketing campaigns and those inventory miscalculations translate to oversells and missed[delivery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhivery) dates, lost revenue as well as disgruntled customers.


An ideal inventory management system ensures that D2C brands have the optimum inventory levels, directs multiple sales channels and leads to improved purchasing decisions.

## Table of Contents Inventory Management for a D2C Brand


Inventory management refers to the process of tracking the goods and services a company purchases, stores, sells and then returns.


If you are a D2C brand this process might go like:


- Finished products and individual SKUs
- Stock stored across multiple warehouses
- Website and marketplace inventory
- Product bundles and kits
- Returned and exchanged products
- Damaged or unsellable inventory
- Reserved stock for pending orders
- In-transit inventory


The goal is simple: to have the right products at the right time and not hold unnecessary inventory.


## Why Multi-Channel Inventory Management Matters


Many D2C brands sell through multiple channels at once. Imagine a skincare brand selling through its own Shopify store, Amazon, Instagram and its offline pop-up stores all at the same time.


Without a centralized inventory, the same physical inventory may be inadvertently reserved for multiple customers.


Lets say a brand has 100 volume of a product out there. For example, the website may list 60 units being available but it also lists another 50 units on a marketplace,[functions of inventory management](https://getswipe.in/blog/article/functions-of-inventory-management) so the business receives orders from customers for 110 units when there are only actually 100.


This is exactly why inventory should be the most synchronized across every selling channel.


An inventory function that centralizes the stock and gets updated whenever any order is placed, canceled, returned or fulfilled. Both help to reduce overselling, giving a clearer picture of available stock.


## October 2023 data only


Assign a unique SKU for every variation of a product whenever possible.


For instance, a T-shirt offering three sizes and four colors would have its own SKU for every possible combination. This means the business knows which variation is selling and which variation is sitting in inventory.


SKU-level tracking helps businesses:


- Monitor fast- and slow-moving products
- Identify popular product variations
- Reduce picking and packing errors
- Forecast future demand
- Reorder goods at right time


This is particularly pertinent when products are sold as bundles.


## Managing Product Bundles and Kits


Making bundles is a common D2C brand strategy to boost average order value and promote product bundling — when customers buy several products together.


On the other hand, bundles can make inventory management a little more difficult.


Imagine a beauty brand sells:


- Face wash
- Moisturizer
- Sunscreen


It might also be available as a “Complete Skincare Kit,” which includes all three products.


More specifically, the bundle should not always be a physical item. The inventory of it relies upon the abundance of the separate items inside it.


So for 20 face washes, 15 moisturizers and 10 sunscreens, you could only make a max of 10 complete kits.


Thus, inventory systems should learn about bundle components instead of treating every bundle as independent stock.


Brands must specify what a bundle includes, in which quantities, using what SKUs and how it will be stocked before creating one.


## Handling Returns and Exchanges Correctly


Returns constitutes the major inventory problem for D2C businesses.


If the customer returns a product, it should not immediately appear on the available products. You need to gauge its state first.


Returned products widely fall broadly in the following categories:


Saleable: the product is unopened and in a state that allows for resale


**Open Box:** The product may be sold on discount.


**Damaged:** The product is unusable and needs to be thrown away or repaired


**Quality Check needed:** The product requires an inspection prior to returnable inventory.


This helps nothing but makes certain that the only products released for new orders are within an in-depth return workflow.


In case of exchanges the system should also take into account both, the product that is returned along with the one that replaces it. If not, stock quantities can be misleading.


## Separate Available, Reserved and Damaged Stock


The easiest way to increase inventory accuracy? Break down the stock into meaningful categories


For example:


- **Available stock:** Ready to sell
- **Reserved stock:** Designated for orders that are confirmed
- **In-transit stock:** Moving between locations
- **Returned stock:** Awaiting inspection
- **Damaged stock:** Unfit for sale
- **Quarantine stock:** Reserved for quality checks.


This discourages businesses from taking the liberty of assuming every material unit can be put up for sale at any given moment.


## Set Reorder Levels


If you run out of your best-selling product, it means lost sales and consumers who are frustrated. On the other side of that coin, overordering means locking cash you could use for other things.


Find reorder points for your important SKUs of D2C brands


For example, a reorder point can be based on:


- Average daily sales
- Supplier lead time
- Seasonal demand
- Safety stock
- Upcoming promotions
- Historical sales trends


To take an instance, if the brand sells roughly 20 units a day and its supplier takes 10 days to deliver then it should plan well before the stock gets exhausted.


And automated low-stock alerts can simplify this process.


## Use One Source of Truth


The more effective approach in inventory management is to not have multiple spreadsheets or different systems for various sales channels.


Rather, businesses should be striving for a single source of inventory that ties their ecommerce platform to marketplaces, warehouses, order management system and accounting process where applicable.


This allows you to get a single view of stock and minimises manual entry.


You can also use automation to update inventory after sales, cancellations, refunds, returns and stock transfers.


## Conduct Regular Inventory Reconciliation


Although assisted by automation, inventory discrepancies can still arise from damaged products, incorrect shipments, robbery/exposure to theft, counting errors and system issues.


Stock reconciliation recognises these differences.


Businesses can compare:


**System Inventory + System Adjustments = Physical Inventory**


Therefore if numbers do not match they should be investigated rather than just amended without knowing what caused them to differ.


Cycle counting, where you check selected SKUs instead of everything at once, can help without halting operations.


## Conclusion


Inventory management is extremely vital to maintain for a D2C brand, especially as they look to scale their operations.


When it comes to multi-channel stock, bundles, returns + exchanges and/or inventory categories, you need way more than a spreadsheet. One can centrally and through automation get better access on stock errors, delivery fulfillment stats with a timely view and avoid unnecessary inventory costs.


With the scaling of a D2C brand, so should its inventory management. Incorporating accurate SKU tracking, clean return processes, bundle rules, reorder points and regular reconciliation into the operational flow can help to create the scaffolding on which true sustainable growth is built.


# ‍ **FAQs:**


### **1. What is even inventory management for a D2C brand?**


For a D2C brand, inventory management means keeping track of your products across sales channels, warehouses (if you have multiple), product bundles (if applicable), orders, returns & exchanges to ensure that the stock levels are always correct.


### **2. What is D2C Multi-channel Inventory Management and why is it Important?**


It also synchronises stock between sites, marketplaces, social commerce sites and other channels, alleviating overselling, stockouts & inventory errors.


### **3. Managing product bundles is one of the factors that D2C brands are faced with.**


A bundler tracks individual SKUs that make the whole in D2C brands wise. Bundles should really only be available based on the inventory levels of its components and shouldn’t be used as independent inventory.


### **4. How to add returned products back in stock?**


Returned items must be examined and put into categories such as resaleable, open-box damaged, or quality-check later. Which products should be restocked — include only those that are eligible


### **5. What is the difference between available inventory and reserved in inventory?**


Available inventory is for sale and reserved inventory has been allocated to customer orders—never to be sold to other customers.


### **6. Inventory stockouts are a common issue that D2C brands face** .


Based on the sales velocity, supplier lead times, seasonal demand and safety stock brands can set reorder points. It can also help indicate when to replenish stock before the inventory goes low.


### **7. How to keep the D2C inventory accurate?**


Having accurate inventory can be made easy with a centralized inventory management, synchronization of multiple sales channels, tracking products using SKU, proper return management and regular inventory reconciliation.
